sourceBindings.text: A colour or number from a soil test is useful only when you know what was extracted, how it was measured, its unit and the crop-specific interpretation. Watch the trainer's demonstration, then explain the evidence and the missing information before considering a fertilizer recommendation.
Put extraction, filtration, reagent reaction and reading in order, and explain what the demonstrated method can and cannot measure.
Read pH, organic-matter percentage and nutrient results with their units, methods and crop-specific reference; distinguish an extracted test index from total soil reserves and a fertilizer rate.
Identify the missing method, local interpretation, crop, field and product information that prevents a universal NPK class or amount; leave X and Y as unknowns until supported.

sourceBindings.text: A trainer shows a rapid P kit: measured soil is mixed with extractant, filtered, reacted and read against its chart. A learner says the colour measures all P in the field.
Put the four stages in their observed order and name the method-specific quantities and reagent from the kit instructions, rather than inventing them.
The colour or instrument represents the fraction and response defined by that method, not total P in the soil.
A crop decision also needs the kit or laboratory's calibrated interpretation and field context.
A test index acquires meaning through its method and calibration.

sourceBindings.text: A classroom report shows pH 5.5 and P 12 ppm. Someone copies the example table and writes 'apply X lime and Y fertilizer' without knowing either amount.
Under that table, the values fall in its low rows. Say 'under that table' because the table has no method or regional calibration.
Ask for crop target and lime requirement, and for the P extraction method and suitable local recommendation.
Keep X and Y blank until those inputs, product analyses and application conditions are known.
A classroom class is not a field application rate.

sourceBindings.text: A report says only 'P 18 ppm' and a learner labels it Low using the classroom table.
18 falls in the table's 15–20 ppm gap, so the example provides no category even on its own terms.
The extraction method, sample basis, crop and regional guide are absent, so a different table cannot be borrowed casually.
Request the laboratory's interpretation; do not choose a P fertilizer or amount from this number alone.
An honest 'unclassified with this evidence' is more useful than a confident guess.

sourceBindings.text: A learner sees a P soil-test result of 12 ppm and a bag labelled 11-52-0. They claim the bag will add 52 ppm of soil P.
The soil report's ppm result has a method and sample basis; it is not a product percentage.
11-52-0 gives percentages of N, P2O5 and K2O in the product, not a direct change in soil-test P.
Rate requires a calibrated crop nutrient recommendation, product content, area and application method, with any credits and limits.
Keep soil-test units and fertilizer-product analysis separate.

sourceBindings.text: extractant
A solution specified by a test method to release a defined fraction of a soil constituent for measurement.
filtrate
The liquid obtained after separating particles from the soil suspension in the stated method.
colour reaction
A method-specific reagent reaction whose colour can be compared with a chart or measured by a suitable instrument.
ppm
Parts per million on the report's stated mass or volume basis; ask whether the result is mg/kg soil, mg/L solution or another declared basis.
calibration
The method- and region-specific link between a test index and crop response or category.
N-P-K label
Fertilizer percentages of N, phosphate as P2O5 and potash as K2O; not the soil-test ppm values.
